title: Hospitality to guests
hook: the guest is honored; the door stays open

segments.voice: Yesterday, food as theology: one row, one pot, even for an emperor. Your line was equality at the table. Who did you notice at your table, and who was missing? Day one thousand four hundred sixteen.

Ji aayan nu. It's a Punjabi welcome, said at the door, sometimes with both hands pressed together, and a question follows close behind: tea? Then the kettle is already on. A guest arrives, and the house rearranges itself around them. The good cup comes out. Someone gives up the best chair. It's a small, ordinary scene. In Sikh teaching, though, it rests on something larger than manners. Yesterday was the meal. Today is the door, and the idea that it shouldn't be closed to anyone.
screen: `JI AAYAN NU: WELCOME.` → `THE KETTLE IS ALREADY ON.` → `TODAY, THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, the reason. In a hymn in Raag Majh, Guru Arjan says to God, in paraphrase, that all are called sharers in Your household, and You are seen as outside of no one. The Punjabi word is saanjhivaal: partners, people who share. If God is within everyone, then no guest is a stranger. Second, the building. The Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the Golden Temple, is a place Sikhs hold dear, and tradition says its doors open on every side, as a sign that people from every direction are welcome. Whatever you believe, whatever you're called, there's a way in from where you're standing. Third, what the gurdwara does with that. Alongside the langar, some gurdwaras keep rooms where travelers can rest, and anyone can come in, cover their head, and sit. The guest is honored by being given what the house has: food, shade, a place on the floor with everyone else. Fourth, the cost. An open door is not always comfortable. It lets in people who are loud, or sad, or not like us. Keeping it open means deciding ahead of time that the person who knocks is welcome before you know who they are. That's hard to practice when the doorbell rings and you're tired. But it's what the hymn is pointing at: if God is outside of no one, the door has no one to close against.
screen: `SAANJHIVAAL: NO ONE IS AN OUTSIDER.` · `DOORS ON EVERY SIDE, TRADITION SAYS.` · `FOOD, SHADE, A PLACE ON THE FLOOR.` · `WELCOME BEFORE YOU KNOW WHO KNOCKS.` · then, large: `THE DOOR STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome a guest. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who might come through your door, or your inbox, or your desk, this week: a visitor, a new coworker, a neighbor you've only waved at. Breathe in, and see them arriving. Breathe out, and decide, before they get there, that they're welcome. Then choose one small thing you'll offer: a drink, a chair, a few minutes of real attention, their name said properly. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Hospitality to guests. The guest is honored because, as Guru Arjan sings, all are sharers, and God is outside of no one. Today's word.

Your line: the door stays open. Today, when someone interrupts you, treat them as a guest for the first minute: look up, say their name, and offer them something. Day one thousand four hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Gurdwaras welcome anyone who comes, of any faith or none, asking that visitors cover their heads and remove their shoes; Sikh households traditionally greet guests with food and tea.
